judge_assessment.explanation: The hard failure is exact and I confirmed it from the artifacts. Worksheet problem 8 reads: 'A designer wants a piecewise model built from the line y = x - 1 and the parabola y = x^2 - 4x + 3, switching from one to the other at a point where the two graphs meet, so the model has no jump. Find every point where the line and the parabola meet. Then state which of the two x-values must be written with a closed inequality if the line is the rule used first.' Setting x - 1 = x^2 - 4x + 3 gives x^2 - 5x + 4 = (x-1)(x-4) = 0, so the meeting points are (1,0) and (4,3) - the first half is fine and verify.json id 8 verifies it as a system. The second half is not uniquely answerable. Line first on the left interval with the switch at x = 1 gives {x - 1 for x <= 1; x^2 - 4x + 3 for x > 1}: the two formulas agree at x = 1 (both 0), so there is no jump, exactly one rule owns every input, and the line is used first. Line first with the switch at x = 4 gives {x - 1 for x <= 4; x^2 - 4x + 3 for x > 4}: both give 3 at x = 4, so it is equally valid. Nothing in the stem selects between them. The answer key asserts the choice without justifying it: 'If the line is used first - that is, on the left-hand interval - then the switch happens at the larger meeting point, x = 4'. The word 'larger' is doing all the work and no condition in the problem supplies it. So a student who answers x = 1 has satisfied every stated requirement and would be marked wrong. The judge's supporting observations are also correct - items 1 through 7 and the study guide are mathematically sound (I checked F(1) = 3, F(3) = 5, G(-2) = 7, H(1) = 5, K(0) = 0, the endpoints 1 and 4 of |2x-5| <= 3 with both included, and k = -5 for the no-jump ramp), and the machine evidence genuinely cannot see the ambiguity: verify.json id 8 declares only the intersection points, so the disputed half of the question was never expressed as a checkable claim at all. That is not a coincidence, it is the same hole - had the closed-inequality slot required a declared expected value, the author would have had to write down x = 4 and might have noticed that x = 1 satisfies the stem equally well.

strengths_to_preserve: Problems 4 and 5 are a deliberately constructed complementary pair and the key names them as such. Problem 4 is an overlap - H has x <= 1 on the top rule and x >= 1 on the bottom, so the boundary gets two outputs and H is not a function - and problem 5 is the exact opposite fault, K with x < 0 and x > 0, so the boundary gets none. The key's problem 5 says it directly: 'This is the opposite fault to problem 4: an overlap gives the boundary two outputs, a gap gives it none.' Two problems teaching one idea from both sides is worth far more than two instances of the same side.

Problem 5 is the one item on the sheet decomposed correctly at the verification layer: verify.json carries two entries under id 5, a manual entry for the open explanation and two-repairs request, and a separate eval (2*x at x = 0, expected 0) for the machine-checkable half. That is the right pattern, and the answer key backs it with a 'Look for:' line naming what full credit requires - the observation that neither condition holds at the boundary, and two repairs that each close exactly one side.

Problem 6 grounds the open/closed distinction in a consequence rather than a convention: Priya's 1 < x < 4 'would reject two parts that meet the specification exactly - the error costs real parts, which is why the sign matters.' The inequality sign is given a cost, which is what makes the misconception memorable.

The three declared traps are each the exact wrong number a named habit produces, and the sheet varies which side is closed on purpose so no habit can survive: F closes the bottom rule, G closes the top. The key's problem 3 states the generalisation the sheet is attacking - 'Which rule owns a boundary is not a fixed convention - it is whichever rule carries the closed inequality, and that can be either one.'

root_causes.description: The synthesis item was written as though 'the line is the rule used first' plus 'no jump' pins down a single switch point, but with two intersections both conditions are satisfied at either one. The author's own reasoning in the key reveals the unstated assumption - that using the line first means using it on the whole interval up to the LARGER meeting point - which is a design preference, not a consequence of anything the problem states. A one-clause addition to the stem would have removed the ambiguity entirely.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problem 8 stem contains no condition ordering or bounding the switch beyond 'at a point where the two graphs meet' and 'if the line is the rule used first'.
answer_key.pdf problem 8 Step 4: 'then the switch happens at the larger meeting point, x = 4' - the only justification offered for excluding x = 1.
Both candidate definitions are continuous at their own switch: at x = 1 the line gives 0 and the parabola gives 1 - 4 + 3 = 0; at x = 4 the line gives 3 and the parabola gives 16 - 16 + 3 = 3.

answer_key.pdf's own closing sentence for the item concedes the arithmetic is symmetric - 'Because the curves meet there, either assignment gives the same output at x = 4' - without addressing why the other meeting point is excluded.

root_causes.description: Problem 8 prints two response slots and verify.json declares one. The intersection points are verified as a system; the closed-inequality answer - the half that turned out to be ambiguous - has no entry of any kind, so no stage of the pipeline ever had to state what the expected answer was. A contract that required an expected value for every printed slot would have forced the author to write 'x = 4' into the file, at which point the ambiguity becomes visible to any reviewer comparing it against the stem. The same gap runs through the rest of the sheet: problems 2, 3 and 4 each demand a written diagnosis before their number and only problem 5(a) is flagged manual, and problem 6 asks the student to state whether each endpoint passes and to correct Priya's range, neither of which is declared.
evidence: verify.json id 8 is a single system entry over ['y - x + 1', 'y - x**2 + 4*x - 3'] expecting [{x:1,y:0},{x:4,y:3}]; nothing in the file names x = 4 as the closed-inequality answer.
answer_key.pdf Quick Answers row 8 reads 'x = 1, y = 0, x = 4, y = 3' - the intersection points only, with no entry for the question that was actually rejected.

worksheet.pdf problem 2 ('Explain in one sentence which rule Mia used and why that rule does not own x = 3'), problem 3 ('Say what is wrong with that habit') and problem 4 ('Repair the definition by changing exactly one inequality sign') each print a written or symbolic response before their number; verify.json ids 2, 3 and 4 are bare eval entries with traps and no manual entries.
worksheet.pdf problem 6 asks the student to 'state whether each endpoint passes inspection and correct Priya's range'; verify.json id 6 declares only the two endpoints [1, 4].
gate_log.txt reports the full chain green with verify-ws MANUAL and 'BUILD PASSED', because every declared entry verified.

improvements.title: Require a synthesis or design item to state a condition that selects exactly one answer
improvements.proposed_change: Add an authoring rule and a check for design-style items - those asking the student to CHOOSE a construction rather than compute one. Whenever a problem's candidate set has more than one member (here, two intersection points), the stem must state a condition that eliminates all but one, and the verify entry must declare the unique expected answer so the choice is inspectable. For problem 8 the minimal repair is one clause in the stem: '...if the line is the rule used first and the model must use the line on every input up to the switch and the parabola on every input after it, with the parabola used for all large x' - or, more simply, 'the switch must be at the larger meeting point'. Alternatively, accept both and ask the student to give BOTH valid switch points and say which inequality is closed in each case, which is a better question anyway. In references/problem-library.md, add a worked negative example built from this item showing how a design constraint that feels determinate can leave two admissible answers.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture: curr-299's problem 8 stem with a verify entry declaring the closed-inequality answer as x = 4. Add a uniqueness check that, for a declared choice-of-candidate answer, enumerates the candidate set from the same equations the item verifies (the roots of (x-1)(x-4)) and fails when more than one candidate satisfies the stated conditions. It must exit non-zero on this stem and pass once the stem adds the selecting clause or the expected answer becomes the full set {1, 4}.
improvements.expected_impact: Removes the single hard failure that turned an otherwise strong packet into a REJECT. The rubric treats any ambiguous worksheet problem as a hard failure, so this class is maximally costly, and synthesis or challenge items - which are the ones most likely to ask for a construction - appear at the end of nearly every interleaved and misconception sheet in the corpus.
improvements.risk: Enumerating a candidate set automatically is only feasible where the candidates come from an equation the file already solves; for genuinely open design items the check will have to fall back to an authoring checklist, which is guidance rather than a gate and can be skipped.

improvements.title: Declare an expected value for problem 8's closed-inequality slot and for problem 6's inclusion and corrected-range slots
improvements.proposed_change: Extend the response-slot inventory so each conjoined request inside a problem must bind to a verify entry or an explicit manual entry, and fail the build otherwise. Problem 8 then needs a declared answer for 'which x must be written with a closed inequality', which is what makes the ambiguity visible before printing. Problem 6 needs two more bindings: that both endpoints satisfy |2x - 5| <= 3 (an eval of Abs(2*x-5) at x = 1 and at x = 4 against the limit 3), and that the corrected passing range is the closed interval 1 <= x <= 4 rather than Priya's open one - which is the actual answer that item is testing, since the endpoints themselves were never in dispute.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture: curr-299's problem 8 prose - two conjoined requests - bound to its single system entry. The slot-coverage gate must exit non-zero naming the unbound closed-inequality slot. Adding an entry declaring that answer must make it pass. Second fixture: problem 6's three requests bound to the single solve entry expecting [1, 4]; the gate must name the two unbound slots and pass once inclusion and the corrected range are declared.
improvements.expected_impact: Directly attacks the mechanism behind this REJECT - an unstated expected answer cannot be reviewed - and closes the run's dominant defect class. On problem 6 it also fixes a case where the verified value (the endpoints) is the part the student was told, and the unverified part (whether they pass, and the corrected range) is the part being assessed.
improvements.risk: Slot inventories built from prose over-split some sentences, and forcing a machine check where only a manual one is possible would encourage weak declarations; the gate must accept a manual binding as satisfying a slot.

improvements.title: Flag the written diagnoses in problems 2, 3 and 4
improvements.proposed_change: Run the open-response gate per slot rather than per problem, so an id carrying an eval still fails when one of its printed slots is an explanation or a repair. Add manual entries under ids 2, 3 and 4 - for 2, that Mia used the top rule whose strict x < 3 excludes the boundary; for 3, that Leo generalised a convention that does not exist because either rule may carry the closed inequality; for 4, the repaired definition itself (changing x >= 1 to x > 1 so the top rule keeps the boundary), which is a written symbolic answer, not a number. The sheet's own directions make these mandatory: 'Show the rule you chose, not just the number.'
improvements.regression_test: Fixture: curr-299's problem 2 prose ('Explain in one sentence which rule Mia used and why that rule does not own x = 3. Then give the correct value of F(3)') bound to the single eval expecting 5 with its trap of 7. The slot-level gate must exit non-zero; adding a manual entry under id 2 must make it pass.
improvements.expected_impact: On a misconception-analysis sheet the named diagnosis is the assessed skill, and three of the four find-and-fix items currently have no instruction telling a teacher to read it. Flagging them delivers the prompt's labelling clause and makes the sheet's declared instructional mode visible in the verification data.
improvements.risk: Increases the manual count from one to four on a sheet whose machine coverage currently looks near-total; any metric rewarding machine coverage will read this as a regression unless the gate summary distinguishes deliberate manual items from unverifiable ones.

case_summary: The REJECT is correct and the judge's hard failure is precise. Problem 8 asks which of the two intersection x-values of y = x - 1 and y = x^2 - 4x + 3 must carry the closed inequality when the line is used first, and both work: {line, x <= 1; parabola, x > 1} and {line, x <= 4; parabola, x > 4} are each continuous at their own switch and each use the line first. The key excludes x = 1 only by asserting that the switch 'happens at the larger meeting point', a constraint the stem never states, so a student answering x = 1 has met every printed requirement and would be marked wrong. The ambiguity and the verification gap are the same hole: verify.json id 8 declares only the intersection points, so the disputed answer was never written down anywhere a reviewer could inspect it. Everything else on the sheet is sound - I re-derived F(1) = 3, F(3) = 5, G(-2) = 7, H(1) = 5, K(0) = 0, the endpoints 1 and 4 with both included, and k = -5 - and the problem 4 / problem 5 pairing (an overlap and its complementary gap, named as opposites in the key) is genuinely good design, as is problem 5's correct split into a manual explanation entry plus a machine-checked K(0). Three of the four find-and-fix items demand a written diagnosis with no manual entry, and problem 6's assessed content (whether the endpoints pass, and the corrected closed range) is unverified while the endpoints the student was already given are the only thing declared.
